Several specialized raw material inputs represent potential bottlenecks for LPT production: Grain-oriented electrical steel: GOES is the single most important input for transformer cores, yet U.S. supply is constrained both in grade variety and manufacturing capacity. Cleveland- Cliffs is the only GOES manufacturer in the United States operating two production facilities. The Cleveland-Cliffs facilities produce limited quantities of conventional Hi-B grade GOES, which is preferred for LPT cores because of lower core losses and higher magnetic efficiency. As a result, U.S. manufacturers frequently import premium-grade GOES; imported GOES is typically processed by U.S. core fabrication companies where it is laminated before being integrated into transformers by original equipment manufacturers. Copper: CTCs for windings require high-quality oxygen-free copper (Dubey 2017). The United States consumes close to 1.6 million metric tons of copper annually (U.S. Geological Survey 2025). The majority of U.S. copper mining occurs in Arizona, and scrap recovery provides close to one-third the U.S. supply. Approximately 75% of mine production is refined domestically. Superior Essex (headquartered in Georgia) and Rea Magnet Wire (based in Indiana) are the primary U.S. producers of supply magnet wire and rectangular conductors for transformers in North America (Guidehouse 2022). However, for CTCs, which are a critical component of LPT windings, Sam Dong is the only domestic manufacturer.3 This reliance on a single U.S. supplier creates a supply chain bottleneck, prompting original equipment manufacturers to turn to imported CTC. OLTC: Reinhausen is the only U.S. OLTC producer. ABB/Hitachi and Reinhausen also operate factories in Europe that supply compatible units.
